title: seva as vocation
hook: after a long fast, a king finally sits down to a meal, and the guests start arriving

segments.voice: Yesterday, seva as vocation came from the trees: life, wealth, understanding and words, given to whoever asks. Which of the four did you give? Day one thousand two hundred ten.
screen: `LIFE, WEALTH, UNDERSTANDING, WORDS.` · `A KING AT HIS TABLE.`

segments.voice: A king who has already given away everything he owns sits down to eat. He and his family have gone a long stretch without food, without even water. Now, at last, there's a meal in front of them: a little ghee, some milk, a porridge, a cup of water. Hands reach for the bowls. And then someone comes to the door. The king's name is Rantideva, and the Bhagavata's ninth book tells this story in a handful of verses. It's a short story. It doesn't feel short when you're the one holding the bowl.
screen: `A LONG FAST, THEN A MEAL.` → `SOMEONE AT THE DOOR.` → `RANTIDEVA.`

segments.voice: The first to come is a brahmin guest. Rantideva sees God in his guest and feeds him gladly, and the guest eats and goes. Rantideva divides what's left with his family, and another guest arrives, a laborer, and he feeds him too. Then comes a man with a pack of hungry dogs, and Rantideva gives him the rest of the food, honoring the man and the dogs alike. Now only water is left. And one more person comes, a man his society shut out as an outcaste, dying of thirst, asking for water. Rantideva, nearly dying of thirst himself, gives it. Then he says the words the story is remembered for. In paraphrase: I don't ask God for the highest state, with all its powers, nor even for freedom from rebirth. I ask to stand inside all beings and bear their pain, so that they can be free of it. The story ends with a turn. The guests, it says, were the lords of the worlds themselves, come in disguise. They reveal themselves, ready to grant anything. Rantideva bows, and asks for nothing. Notice two things for a vocation of seva. First, every guest gets the same honor. The story lines them up from the honored to the shunned, and the king's care doesn't shrink as he goes down the line. Second, he doesn't serve to get somewhere. Not heaven, not even freedom. The service is the destination.
screen: `GUEST AFTER GUEST, THE SAME HONOR.` · `ONLY WATER LEFT, AND HE GIVES IT.` · `NOT HEAVEN, NOT FREEDOM: THEIR PAIN.` · `THE GUESTS WERE THE GODS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the guests come. Settle, and breathe. Picture a table with a small meal on it, yours. One at a time, let people you know come to the door: someone easy to give to, then someone harder, then someone you'd usually walk past. You don't have to hand anything over. Just notice the moment of reluctance with each one, and breathe through it. If you pray, you can hold each guest before the One you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Seva as vocation. Service as a whole life: Rantideva gives each guest the same honor, down to the last cup of water, and asks nothing back. Today's word.
Your line: seva as vocation. Today, serve one person you'd usually walk past with the care you'd give a guest of honor. Day one thousand two hundred ten.

howItsDone: Rantideva's story from the Bhagavata's ninth book is told by Hindu teachers as a picture of selfless service, and his wish to bear the pain of all beings is quoted in talks on compassion and seva.

fork.setup: you're Rantideva. after a long fast, only water is left, and you're dying of thirst. a man at the door begs for water. what do you do?
options: give him half and keep half.
fork.reveal: he gives it all, and says he asks not for heaven or freedom but to bear the pain of all beings so they can be free of it.

original.note: Sanskrit: the name of the king in the Bhagavata's ninth book who gave his last food and water to his guests.

trapdoor: what you thought: service is a step toward your own salvation.
what it means: in Rantideva's words, service that wants nothing for itself, not even freedom, only others' relief.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavata Purana 9.21.12, na kamaye 'ham gatim ishvarat param: the king declines the highest goal and asks to bear the suffering of all embodied beings.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 9.21.2–10 (Rantideva's fast; the meal; the brahmin, the shudra, the man with dogs, the pulkasa asking for water)
Bhagavata Purana 9.21.12–13 (I do not desire the highest goal with its powers, nor freedom from rebirth; I take on the suffering of all beings so they may be free of it)
Bhagavata Purana 9.21.15–17 (the guests were the lords of the worlds; Rantideva asks for nothing)

notes: The text gives the length of the fast as a number of days; the script says 'a long stretch' instead. Confirm the meal items (ghee, milk-porridge, a barley preparation, water).

The guests are rendered as 'a brahmin guest', 'a laborer' (shudra), 'a man with a pack of hungry dogs', and 'a man his society ranked lowest of all' (pulkasa). A Keeper should check this caste framing.
9.21.12 paraphrased; trapdoor transliteration 'na kamaye 'ham gatim ishvarat param' should be confirmed.
The guests' identity at 9.21.15 (the lords of the three worlds, appearing through Vishnu's maya) is summarized as 'the gods themselves, testing him'; confirm.
howItsDone is a general description; confirm or soften.

Editor pass: 'a man his society ranked lowest of all' (an unsourced superlative) became 'a man his society shut out as an outcaste'; 'the gods themselves, testing him' became 'the lords of the worlds themselves, come in disguise' (the testing motive is not in 9.21.15 as cited); 'the ones his world looked past' became 'the shunned' to avoid repeating day 1207's phrase.
